item.title: The Dolly Parton Effect Is a Bridge in a Divided World
item.description:
Authenticity

The Dolly Parton Effect Is a Bridge in a Divided World

In a divided world, Dolly had a unique ability to bring people together.

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • Dolly drew diverse crowds across political and cultural divides through shared human connection.
  • Her music has a uniquely high percentage of positive words, even about heavy topics.
  • She united people by sharing deeply specific personal stories in a positive way.
Source: Sahroe Shutterstock

The world is in mourning. The flags are at half-mast, the Empire State Building is lit up with sparkly pink lights, and tributes from politicians, musicians, actors, and regular folks are flooding social media. Other than Dolly Parton, who could inspire this level of grief? She was that rare celebrity who everyone loved, and her passing has left a huge hole in the hearts of not just her most ardent fans, not just the American country music industry, but pretty much everyone, everywhere.

Her ability to bring vastly different people together was undeniable, a phenomenon I witnessed firsthand about 10 years ago. It was a warm, late-summer evening and I had joined about 16,000 other people in an open-air amphitheatre on the shore of Lake Ontario to see Dolly in concert. There was an energy to the crowd, a giddy level of excitement that seemed a bit different than a typical concert crowd, and definitely different than one might expect for a then-70-year-old country star. There were a few cowboy hats and boots, but there were just as many sparkly blouses, feather boas, and thigh-high boots. People wore sensible shoes and cardigans, teenagers in retro Dolly T-shirts, and a few denim-on-denim Canadian tuxedos. Drag queens were dressed as Dolly, in big blond wigs and covered in sequins. Families came with young children, groups of friends, and couples young and old. It was a glittery and colourful cross-section of humanity, drawn together by nostalgia, for sure, but also something else.

When Dolly walked out on stage, the rhinestones on her dress and her guitar caught the light; she literally glowed. The cheers were loud enough to carry across the lake. Of course, the show was incredible. Her voice was pure and sweet, a perfectly pitched country twang with that distinctive vibrato. She was entertaining, funny, a little sassy, a bit corny; everything you’d expect from Dolly the Legend. But as amazing as the show was, what stood out the most was what was happening in the crowd.

When Dolly was onstage, her warmth, humour, and openness seemed to reach everyone at once, no matter who they were. When she sang of her pride and faith in the face of childhood bullying in Coat of Many Colours, for those three minutes everyone in the audience knew exactly how it felt to be teased about something they valued. It was the same with the wistful hometown pride of My Tennessee Mountain Home, the poignant desperation of Jolene, and the misery of the corporate grind in 9 to 5. They were Dolly’s stories, but they were also our stories. The more specifically she described them, the more universal they were. In those moments, everyone in the amphitheatre felt that Dolly was singing just to them.

To understand why her stories resonate so universally, my colleagues Danielle Law and Avnee Sharma and I conducted a study analyzing the mechanics of her songwriting (Eaton and colleagues, 2025). Rather than study broad themes, we focused on how she said it, not so much what she said: the kinds of words she used to tell those stories. We analyzed the lyrics of every song Dolly wrote independently between 1967 and 2020, comparing them with the top 10 songs from the Billboard country and pop charts across those same years. Using linguistic analysis (Pennebaker and colleagues, 2022), we calculated the percentage of words conveying positive emotional tone (love, joy, happy) versus negative tone (sad, cry, hate).

Dolly outperformed both pop and country, with a significantly higher percentage of positive language overall. In addition, while the percentage of positive words in both pop and country music has steadily declined over the decades, Dolly’s lyrics were remarkably consistent. There was no decline. It’s not that she doesn’t write about difficult topics; her catalogue includes songs about unplanned pregnancy, mental illness, social justice, bullying, and more. It’s that she approaches heavy, vulnerable topics with an uplifting, hopeful lens.

Obviously, Dolly was popular for many reasons: her personal charisma, her philanthropic endeavours, her sense of humour, and her business acumen. But her distinct ability to frame universal human struggles using positive, optimistic language may also have played a role.

Dolly’s passing has temporarily transformed strangers into a community united by shared grief. It’s one thing to do this when your fan base is already relatively homogenous and shares a common worldview, but Dolly’s fans could easily find topics to disagree on. When you can unite people from opposing political, religious, and cultural backgrounds, especially in a world that seems impossibly divided, you’ve achieved something truly remarkable.

In an increasingly polarized world where people tend to focus on differences rather than similarities, Dolly and her songs bypass our natural psychological defences about in-groups, out-groups, or any groups at all. By singing about highly specific yet universal human struggles, using positive rather than divisive language, Dolly reminds us of the one identity we all share: Our humanity.

Dolly the Legend.
